questions.question: What does the function T(n) represent in running-time analysis?
gold_points: T(n) represents the running time for an input of size n.
It can be interpreted as number of time units or operation count.
It summarizes performance as a function of input size.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF pages 4-5 (book pages 92-93)

questions.question: What are the two principal approaches to summarizing program running time?
gold_points: Benchmarking is one approach for summarizing program running time.
Analysis is the other approach for summarizing program running time.
The chapter focuses mainly on algorithm and program analysis.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: What is a statement counter?
gold_points: A statement counter records how many times each program statement is executed.
It is used on a particular set of inputs.
It differs from a profiler because it counts executions rather than measuring the fraction of total time.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: Why does the chapter use big-oh notation instead of exact time formulas?
gold_points: Big-oh hides constant factors that depend on machine and compiler details.
It focuses on growth behavior rather than exact implementation constants.
It enables clearer comparison of algorithm scalability.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF pages 8-9 (book pages 96-97)

questions.question: Why is simplicity important when choosing an algorithm for long-term use?
gold_points: A simple algorithm is easier to implement correctly.
It is less likely to contain subtle bugs that appear later on unusual inputs.
It is easier for other programmers to understand, document, modify, and maintain.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Why can a linear-time algorithm become preferable to a quadratic-time algorithm as input size grows?
gold_points: A quadratic algorithm can be faster for small inputs because of constant factors.
As input size grows, the lower growth rate of the linear algorithm becomes more important.
For large problems, growth rate matters more than a small constant-factor advantage.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 6 (book page 94)

questions.question: Explain step-by-step how the chapter estimates the running time of a simple for-loop using a numbered list.
gold_points: Bound the time required for one iteration of the loop body.
Multiply that per-iteration bound by the number of iterations.
Treat initialization and final test as lower-order O(1) terms that are usually neglected.
gold_source: Section 3.6 Analyzing the Running Time of a Program, PDF pages 23-24 (book pages 111-112)

questions.question: Explain step-by-step how witnesses are used to prove a big-oh relationship using a numbered list.
gold_points: Choose specific witness values n0 and c.
Show that T(n) is less than or equal to c times f(n).
Verify that the inequality holds for every n greater than or equal to n0.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF page 9 (book page 97)

questions.question: Give a 3-bullet checklist for choosing an algorithm based on the chapter.
gold_points: Check whether the algorithm is easy to understand, implement, and document.
Check whether performance matters for the problem size and available computing resources.
Balance simplicity against efficiency when choosing between possible algorithms.
gold_source: Section 3.1 What This Chapter Is About, PDF page 1 (book page 89)
Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF pages 2-3 (book pages 90-91)
